title: Across the motion, the paper's convention: m gamma squared
spoken: Comoving transverse force over laboratory acceleration gives m gamma squared.
explanation: With the sideways force measured in the electron's own frame and the acceleration in the laboratory, the ratio is m times gamma squared: 1.5625 m at 0.6c. This is the paper's transverse mass.
assumptions: An electron moving along x at speed v in the laboratory, with |v| < c, pushed by a small force.
A force-over-acceleration ratio means nothing until both are labelled with their frames. The paper's transverse mass uses the force measured in the frame moving with the electron.
Modern teaching notation: gamma is the paper's beta, m the electron's mass at rest.

notes.title: m times gamma squared
notes.explanation: The transverse mass as the paper defines it.

notes.title: Force over acceleration, two frames
notes.explanation: The force is from one frame and the acceleration from another; that choice is what gives gamma squared.

notes.title: What it asserts
notes.explanation: The printed transverse mass follows from this convention. The paper's result is not wrong; it answers a question stated with these frames.

notes.title: Lorentz factor
notes.explanation: One over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. At 0.6c it is 1.25.

notes.title: Sideways force, electron's frame
notes.explanation: Measured in the frame moving with the electron at this moment. It is gamma times the laboratory's sideways force.

sentence.text: The sideways force in the electron's frame
